Chapter 7. The Legacy of the Gods: Religion and the Inner Voice.
As those ancient voices slowly faded away, people didn’t just stop believing in gods overnight.
Instead, the whole relationship with the divine started to shift.
The gods, once so present and commanding, moved inward—becoming woven into our private thoughts and feelings. Religion adapted too, finding fresh ways to reach the emerging sense of self.
Picture this:
A priest stands in a grand temple, leading a ritual that used to promise direct conversation with the gods. But now, something’s different. The rituals feel a little emptier, the divine voices more distant than ever.
So, the priest turns inward—to prayer, to meditation, searching for meaning within.
The gods aren’t out there, shouting instructions. They’re inside, offering inspiration, comfort, maybe even a challenge or two.
You can see this change in the stories people began to tell.
Those old epics, packed with gods who controlled every move, slowly gave way to something new—stories of struggle, doubt, and personal transformation.
The spotlight shifted from blind obedience to deeper understanding, from strict rituals to real reflection.
Of course, not everyone was comfortable with this.
The certainty of the old world was gone, replaced by a sense of ambiguity and longing.
But some people saw opportunity.
That inner voice—once so mysterious—became a source of creativity, moral insight, even a way to feel connected to something bigger than yourself.
Religious traditions responded in all sorts of ways.
Some put more emphasis on faith—trusting in a god who was no longer clearly visible or audible.
Others focused on ethics, encouraging people to build virtue and self-control.
Mystics and prophets?
They went searching for direct experiences of the divine, using practices that quieted the inner noise and opened the mind to new kinds of awareness.
What became obvious is this: the gods hadn’t vanished.
They’d simply changed their address.
Now, they lived in the stories we tell ourselves, in the values we hold dear, in the hopes and fears that shape our lives every day.
The legacy of the bicameral mind?
It’s still with us—transformed, but never forgotten.
